name: Two White Eagles

intro.lead: Seven stops round the middle of Saint-Antonin-Noble-Val.
intro.body:
Under a kilometre of walking, about an hour.

Four stops ask a question you can only answer by looking at the thing in front of you. Three just need you standing in the right place.

Built for a Sunday morning, when the market is on. Everything is free. Everything is outdoors except the church, and on a Sunday the church is open.
intro.start: Start on the road bridge over the Aveyron, at the southern edge of the old town, where Rue du Pont de l'Aveyron reaches the water.

outro:
That is the seven.

Now go and sit down. The Cafe de la Halle is on this square and you are thirty metres from it.

If you have walking left, the pale cliff over the town is the Roc d'Anglars and there is a path up it. A stiff climb, and it puts the whole town below you.

topics.name: The Water
topics.blurb: Two rivers meet here. Everything the town has ever done came out of that, including the worst day in its history.

topics.name: Knocked Down, Put Back
topics.blurb: An abbey, a ring of walls and a foreign garrison. Two of the three are gone.

topics.name: The Business of the Town
topics.blurb: Skins, market stalls and the men who ran both. All three are still on the same streets.

stops.title: The Bridge
stops.where: the road bridge over the Aveyron, at the southern edge of the old town

gate.prompt: Get onto the bridge itself, with the river underneath you.

stops.look:
Stand on the bridge, in the middle of it if the traffic lets you.

The big river is the Aveyron. The smaller one joining it is the Bonnette. The pale cliff standing over the town is the Roc d'Anglars.
stops.after:
The town is named after a corpse in a boat.

Antonin was martyred at Pamiers, away south. The story says his body was put in a boat with nobody aboard and two white eagles steered it up this river to here. A monastery went up on the spot in 763 and the town grew round it. Noble Val is the rest of the name. The noble valley.

The two rivers made the place. The Aveyron carried the trade. The Bonnette was small enough to be split into channels and put to work.

They flood, too. In March 1930 the water rose twelve metres and covered three quarters of the town.

stops.title: Inside the Church
stops.where: the parish church, on Place de la Mairie
stops.directions:
Come off the bridge and walk into the town on Rue du Pont de l'Aveyron. The name is on the wall; it is the street the bridge feeds into.

Follow it straight up, about ninety metres, to the square at the top. That is Place de la Mairie.

The church is on the square. Go inside.

question.ask: What time of day has he set it?
question.hint: It is not a daylight scene. Look at what the sky and the water are doing.

stops.look:
One stop indoors, and only because it is Sunday. If a service is running, stay at the back.

On the wall there is a painting of the story you just heard. The boat coming up the river, with the saint's body in it.

Look at the light in it.
stops.after:
Night. It is by Fauconnier, and he painted the whole scene after dark.

Two white eagles is the version most people tell. Some say angels. Either way nobody in the boat is rowing. There is a second version carved over a doorway here by Alex Coutet of Capdenac.

The church is younger than the railway. Begun in 1862, consecrated in 1872. The one it replaced is gone: an abbey stood here from 763 until 1562, when the town turned Protestant, wrecked it and threw the Catholics out.

Louis XIII took the town back in 1622 and pulled the walls down. That is why a medieval walled town has no walls.

Night. It is by Fauconnier, and he painted the whole scene after dark.

Louis the Thirteenth took the town back in sixteen twenty-two and pulled the walls down. That is why a medieval walled town has no walls.

stops.title: Place du Bessarel
stops.where: Place du Bessarel, where the old canal runs through the town
stops.directions:
From Place de la Mairie, go back down Rue du Pont de l'Aveyron a few steps and take the turning right, into the lanes running north west.

Keep going about two hundred metres, towards the sound of running water, until the lane opens into a square with a channel cut through it. That is Place du Bessarel.

question.hint: Look at the stone edge running along the water. It slopes down into it, and it has been worn smooth by something being rubbed on it.

stops.look:
The water crossing this square is not a river. It is a channel, cut on purpose, fed off the Bonnette.

At one side a low open building stands over it, with a long stone basin underneath and a sloping stone edge worn smooth.
stops.after:
Washing clothes. It is a lavoir, the village washhouse, and every French town this size had one.

The channel is older than it looks. It was already the canal du Bessarel in 1315, and this whole quarter ran on it. Tanners, then drapers, because turning hides into leather and washing raw wool both need running water. Saint-Antonin got rich on calfskin in the 1200s and 1300s.

Then the water took it back. The flood of March 1930 destroyed most of the quarter and two people drowned, one of them here. This square only exists because of it, opened on the ground the flood cleared.

One tannery is still standing, a little west of here.

stops.title: The Barracks on Guilhem Peyre
stops.where: the Caserne des Anglais, on Rue Guilhem Peyre
stops.directions:
From Place du Bessarel, take Rue du Pont des Vierges south east out of the square, then turn right onto Rue Amelie Galup and keep straight on into Rue du Cluzel.

About a hundred and seventy metres in all. It brings you out onto Rue Guilhem Peyre.

Walk along it, reading the fronts of the houses.

question.ask: One house on this street was a barracks. Whose soldiers were in it?
question.hint: The house still carries the name, in French, on a plaque or over a door. It is the last word that matters.

stops.look:
One house along here carries a name, carved or painted or on a plaque.

It has been called the same thing for nearly seven hundred years, and the name says who was living in it.
stops.after:
The English. It is the Caserne des Anglais.

English troops were quartered here from 1352 to 1354, in the middle of the Hundred Years War, when this part of France was changing hands over and over. It went on being a barracks long after they left, for the French crown.

They were here two years. The name has lasted nearly seven centuries.

stops.title: The Street of Other People's Things
stops.where: rue de la Pelisserie, running between Place des Tilleuls and Place du Buoc
stops.directions:
From the Caserne, carry on north east along Rue Guilhem Peyre about fifty metres. It runs straight into Rue de la Pelisserie.

Keep going another seventy metres or so, into the middle of the street.

gate.prompt: Get into the middle of Rue de la Pelisserie, in among the shopfronts.

nudge.prompt: Look in the windows as you go, and pick the strangest single object you can find for sale.

stops.look:
Look at the shopfronts, then look above them.

The houses along here are the ones the trade paid for, and a good many are medieval under the paint. On a Sunday you see them over the top of a cheese stall.
stops.after:
Pelisserie means pelts. This was the street of the pelletiers, who dressed skins into fur, and the houses on both sides were theirs and the tanners'. Thirteenth and fourteenth century money. The same trade as Bessarel, one stage on: tanned down by the water, sold up here.

It still sells other people's things. Most of the shops along here are brocante. Furniture, plates, tools, pictures, whatever came out of a house.

On a Sunday the market runs the whole length of it, Place des Tilleuls to Place du Buoc. What is on the stalls tells you the month. Melons and tomatoes now. Truffles and chestnuts in January.

stops.title: The Covered Market
stops.where: the halle, in the main square in the middle of the town
stops.directions:
From Rue de la Pelisserie, walk south down the street to the far end, about a hundred metres. It opens straight into Place de la Halle.

The covered market stands in the middle of the square. Go and get underneath it, in the shade.

gate.prompt: Get right up to the covered market in the middle of the square.

nudge.prompt: The cafes are round the edge of this square and they are open all morning. Pick the one you want now, because you are coming back to it at the end.

stops.look:
Stand under the roof and look up at what is holding it there.

Then look round the square. One building on it is a great deal older than the rest.
stops.after:
The halle went up in 1841 and the town paid for it themselves.

It is still doing its job. Sunday morning, seven until one.

This square also plays a French village in a film. The Hundred-Foot Journey was shot here over nine weeks in the autumn of 2013, with Helen Mirren running a restaurant and Om Puri running the rival one. The scene where the two of them go to the mayor to complain about each other was filmed on this square.

stops.title: The Oldest One
stops.where: the Maison Romane, the old consuls' house on the main square
stops.directions:
From the covered market, cross Place de la Halle to the north west corner, about thirty metres, to the tall stone house with the square tower on top.

Stand back far enough to look up at the row of arches above the ground floor.

question.ask: Who are the two by the tree?
answers: adam and eve and the tree
adam and eve and the serpent
question.hint: Look at the row of small columns in the gallery above the big arches. The flat panels between them are carved. One has a tree with a figure standing on each side of it.

stops.look:
The carvings are the thing here, and they are easy to walk past.

Above the big ground floor arches there is a gallery of small columns with flat carved panels between them. One panel has a man sitting down holding a book. Another has two figures either side of a tree.
stops.after:
Adam and Eve, under the tree. The seated man with the book is the emperor Justinian, holding his law code.

That pairing is not decoration. This building was a court. Justice was done in the hall behind those windows, so they put the first crime and the first law code on the front, where anybody waiting outside could see both.

It went up around 1125 for the viscount of Saint-Antonin and is generally called the oldest civil building in France. Not a church, not a castle. A town house. The consuls bought it in 1312 and ran the town from it until the Revolution.

The tower is not medieval. Viollet-le-Duc invented it in the 1840s, and it is the bit everybody photographs.
